text:
In college, Q could wake from a nap without looking as though he had been asleep. This was among the first things I disliked about him, although I already liked him too much to make use of the information. The rest of us emerged creased and resentful. Q would sit up, put on his shoes, and ask what we thought we might do about dinner.

His name was Quentin, but everyone accepted the letter. It suited his apparent economy: one good coat, one fountain pen, one mild expression adequate to most emergencies.

We met in the laundry room. I had put detergent into a dryer, not because I believed a dryer required detergent, but because I had been thinking about something else.

“What?” Q asked.

I couldn’t remember.

He helped me wipe out the drum. There was no laughter, which made recovery more difficult.

By November, we were eating together four nights a week.

Q listened without preparing a rebuttal and remembered the names of people’s younger siblings. At a party, he caught a falling wineglass by the stem. We discussed it for months. He seemed embarrassed that the catch had become a story, but not embarrassed by having made it.

I studied history; Q studied economics and took enough art classes to make the economics appear voluntary.

Our friendship required few negotiations. Q chose restaurants; I complained about them. Q secured our senior-year house; I made entertaining remarks about the landlord. When the heat failed, Q got it fixed. I developed a theory about the landlord’s childhood.

I was funnier around him. His attention gave my observations a finish they lacked alone.

Still, I watched for evidence. At twenty, I believed intimacy meant obtaining information that contradicted a person’s public character. Once, Q received a B-minus and was quiet through lunch. I felt a disreputable anticipation. Then he said the comments were fair.

We graduated in rain. In the photograph his mother took, Q looks cheerfully wet. I look wronged.

Afterward, friendship thinned through reasonable omissions. His wedding conflicted with my sister’s. A proposed weekend dissolved over train prices. Q joined a cultural foundation; I worked in publishing. Online, I saw photographs of him with a woman named Mara and, eventually, a child. Then I stopped visiting the site.

Nearly ten years passed.

I saw him again at a swimming pool.

That summer, I had rented a room north of the city to finish a book proposal about a nineteenth-century expedition stranded through overconfidence and poor accounting. Each morning I read about their provisions, then bought an elaborate sandwich.

The town pool offered weekly memberships. On my fourth visit, Q came through the gate.

I recognized the way he paused to let it close rather than allowing it to swing back. His hair had receded slightly. A woman in a blue shirt followed him, carrying a notebook.

I sat up, then stopped.

They settled beyond the low hedge bordering my umbrella. I could easily have called his name. Instead, I lowered my sunglasses.

This was not yet a decision to eavesdrop. It was a decision to postpone announcing myself, which is how eavesdropping generally introduces itself.

“I’m sorry to bring it here,” the woman said.

“I’m glad we found a time, Lydia.”

Her contract running the foundation’s education program ended in September. Someone named Stephen had told her the board might fold it into a county partnership.

“Stephen shouldn’t have characterized it that way,” Q said.

“So it isn’t happening?”

“Several things are being considered.”

Lydia opened her notebook.

“I brought the attendance figures. The spring numbers are different if you separate school visits.”

“I’ve seen them.”

“I think that matters.”

“It does.”

His voice was warm, level, faintly confidential. I had heard him use it to persuade campus security that a drunken friend belonged at the health center rather than the police station. Listening, I felt an old relief, as though he might arrange things for both of us.

“The issue isn’t whether you’ve done good work,” he said.

“What is the issue?”

“The funding model isn’t sustainable.”

“But it was never self-supporting. That was the idea. We’re not selling tickets.”

“I know. The board is looking at the organization as a whole.”

“Are you?”

He paused.

“Yes.”

The first answer that seemed to cost him anything.

A whistle announced the hourly break. Wet children hurried past. Q shifted his chair to let a girl through beside the hedge.

I could see his feet, one resting on the other, toes pressed hard against the instep.

“I need to know whether to apply for jobs,” Lydia said. “Now, not September. And my mother’s appointments work with this schedule, but somewhere new—”

She stopped. Q offered no comforting phrase. Briefly, I admired him.

“I don’t want you making plans on the assumption that your contract will be renewed.”

There it was. Plain, regrettable, adequate.

“So that’s what you came to tell me.”

“I wanted to talk before Monday.”

“You could have called.”

“I thought in person was better.”

“At the pool?”

“My daughter’s at the diving workshop. You said you’d be here with your son.”

“I know. I suggested it.”

She closed the notebook.

“Has the board already decided?”

“Not formally.”

“But you have.”

“I don’t decide alone.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He leaned forward.

“My recommendation is not to renew the program in its present form.”

“And me?”

“I don’t think those questions can be entirely separated.”

She laughed without pleasure or surprise.

Q began to speak, then waited. His silences in college had seemed like spaces he deliberately cleared. This one was an interval in which he could find no place to put himself.

“There may be transitional funding,” he said.

“For the program?”

“Possibly. Or a modified role.”

“You’ve looked into that?”

“I’ve had a preliminary conversation.”

“With whom?”

“Stephen.”

She reopened the notebook.

“What did he say?”

“That we could bring it to the board.”

“So there’s a possibility.”

“Of a conversation. I don’t want to overstate it.”

“But if we put together a proposal.”

“I’m not sure there’s time—”

“I can do it this weekend. I sent a partnership version in March. I could update the budget.”

He looked down at his bag. He had come to tell her no and managed instead to assign her work.

“I don’t want you spending your weekend on something that may not—”

“It’s my job. I’d like to spend the weekend trying to keep it.”

A flat slap came from the diving well, followed by applause.

“All right,” Q said.

“I’ll send it Sunday morning.”

“I’ll read it.”

“And circulate it before the meeting?”

“Yes.”

She thanked him. He sat back, then forward again.

“I can’t promise—”

“I understand. I’m not asking for a promise.”

But she had begun smiling, and he seemed unable to bear correcting her again.

They discussed transport costs. Lydia answered with new energy. When she stood, she had a plan for approaching schools.

“I feel better,” she said.

“Well,” Q said.

She touched his arm and left.

He sat on the chair’s edge, elbows on his knees.

For years I had wanted to catch him failing. Now I had no prepared response. I saw the kindness that had undone his attempt, but also its convenience. Lydia would leave hopeful. He had until Sunday before he needed to disappoint her again.

I considered walking around the hedge. We would embrace awkwardly in our insufficient clothes. I would make the book sound further along. He would tell me about the foundation without mentioning Lydia. We might even arrange dinner.

But would I confess what I had heard? Saying nothing meant keeping an advantage he didn’t know I possessed. Telling him meant he would apologize, though he owed me no apology.

A girl of nine ran up, wearing Q’s long mouth and an expression of urgent dissatisfaction.

“Did you see?”

“The last one.”

“Not that one. Before.”

“I’m sorry. I was talking.”

“You were supposed to watch. It was my first backward one.”

“Oh, sweetheart.”

“Don’t call me that.”

“All right.”

She dripped onto his feet. He offered a towel; she turned her shoulder.

“Will you do another?”

“That’s not the point.”

“No,” he said. “I know.”

Neither moved. Then she took the towel.

I put on my shirt while they looked toward the pool. My book had lain open on my stomach, and a damp rectangle marked the page. I packed it carefully, although the damage was done.

At the gate, I glanced back. Q followed his daughter toward the diving well, carrying her sandals. She was explaining something with both hands. He bent his head to listen, and when she stopped walking, he stopped too.

I left without saying hello.
